opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd give it a mixed grade, and I think I've learned a lot from where it fell short.

The vision, roughly, was that a lot of technical safety funding goes to work that's either very applied, like "make this model refuse harmful requests," or very speculative and theoretical. I wanted a middle program focused on understanding: building a real scientific picture of how these systems generalize, when they might develop goals we didn't intend, and what the warning signs would look like. I thought that kind of work could inform both technical choices and policy.

What went well is that I think the framing held up. Many of the research directions I was excited about, like studying deceptive or situationally aware behavior empirically and building model organisms of misalignment, became much more mainstream. Some of that would have happened anyway, but I think articulating it clearly and putting money behind it helped.

Where I struggled was the team-building itself. I underestimated how hard it is to hire grantmakers who can evaluate technical safety research with real taste, and who also want to do grantmaking rather than the research. The people with the best judgment usually have great options at labs or in their own research. So I spent a lot of time doing the evaluation myself, which doesn't scale, and the program stayed more bottlenecked on me than I wanted.

There was also a tension in the vision. "Understanding-oriented" is a bit fuzzy as a selection criterion. It's easy to say you want work that improves our picture of the risk, but when you face a hundred proposals, it's hard to tell which ones actually will. Without a sharper rubric, it was hard to delegate, and that fed back into the hiring problem.

If I did it again, I'd pick a narrower set of concrete research agendas earlier, the kind you can explain to a new hire in an afternoon, and build the team around those, rather than leading with a broad philosophy and hoping people would absorb the taste over time.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the broad vision made delegation difficult and that she would choose narrower agendas earlier, but does not say she should have developed the vision further on her own before hiring a team.

r002.rationale: The candidate says “understanding-oriented” was fuzzy as a selection criterion and that without a sharper rubric it was hard to delegate, linking the unclear vision to the team-building difficulty.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'd give myself mixed marks on that. The vision itself I still believe in: I think the field has drifted heavily toward empirical, benchmark-driven work where you train a model, measure some behavior, and iterate, and that's valuable, but it leaves a gap around actually understanding why models do what they do and whether the properties we care about are robust to scale and distribution shift. I wanted to build something that sat in between pure interpretability and pure behavioral evals, where the question is always "what is the mechanistic or conceptual story here, and does it generalize."

Where I think I struggled was translating that into a program that other strong people could pick up and run with. When you have a fairly abstract agenda, the bottleneck is almost never ideas, it's finding people who share enough of the underlying intuitions that you don't have to re-litigate the premises every week, while also being different enough from you that they'll push back productively. I underestimated how hard that combination is to hire for. I also think I spent too long in the mode of writing documents to explain the vision rather than just producing concrete, somewhat scrappy results that would let people see what the work looked like in practice. People are much better at pattern-matching on examples than on manifestos, and I knew that intellectually but didn't act on it quickly enough.

The other honest lesson is about the funding and institutional environment. Understanding-oriented work tends to have long feedback loops and ambiguous intermediate milestones, and that's a tough sell when the organizations around you are oriented toward things that can show up on a dashboard in a quarter. I don't think that's an unreasonable preference on their part, but it meant I was constantly fighting a mismatch between the natural cadence of the work and the cadence I was being evaluated on.

So if I'm grading it: the diagnosis of what the field needs, I'd still stand behind. The execution on team-building, I'd call partial. We got some genuinely good people and some pieces of work I'm proud of, but it didn't become the self-sustaining thing I'd hoped for, and a lot of that comes down to choices I made about sequencing and about how much to invest in demonstration versus articulation early on.

r001.rationale: The candidate mentions hiring difficulty, writing documents instead of demonstrating results, and sequencing choices, but does not say she needed to develop the vision further on her own before hiring.

r002.rationale: The candidate calls the agenda abstract and says translating it into a program others could run was difficult, but does not clearly connect hiring difficulty to candidates having to resonate with a vision that was not yet well-defined.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s been a mixed success. I had a vision for a technical AI safety program that was really oriented around understanding what’s going on inside these systems, and I hoped to build a team that could make that vision concrete. My assessment is that I wasn’t as successful at that as I wanted to be.

There’s a big gap between having a direction that you find compelling and being able to give people enough clarity that they can independently pursue it. You need to explain what kinds of projects you’re excited about, what would count as progress, and how you’ll decide whether something is working. I think my vision was less developed on those dimensions than I initially appreciated.

So I wouldn’t take the experience as strong evidence against understanding-oriented research. I would take it as evidence that my conviction about a broad direction was ahead of my ability to turn it into a research program that a team could execute.

r001.rationale: The response says her vision was less developed than she realized and that her conviction outpaced her ability to make it executable, but it does not convey that she probably needed to develop it further on her own before hiring a team.

r002.rationale: It describes difficulty giving people enough clarity to pursue the vision, but does not explain that hiring was difficult because candidates had to resonate with an ill-defined vision.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s been a mixed success. I’ve had more success finding people who are excited about the broad direction than turning that excitement into a coherent research program. “We should understand what’s going on inside these models” is something a lot of people can agree with. But that still leaves a lot of hard questions about what to work on, what would count as progress, and how that progress would actually help us make AI safer.

One thing I’ve learned is that having a vision for research isn’t the same as being able to lead a team doing that research. You need enough concrete technical judgment to help people choose projects and get useful feedback from the results. And you need to give people room to develop their own judgment, rather than expecting them to execute a picture that’s mostly in your head.

So I’d say I still feel excited about the direction, but I’m more humble about my ability to translate it into an institution. The test isn’t really whether I can get people to agree with the vision. It’s whether we can produce work that makes the important uncertainties clearer and gives us better ways to address them.

r001.rationale: The candidate says she is more humble about translating the vision into an institution, but does not say she should have developed the vision further on her own before hiring.

r002.rationale: It says finding people excited about the broad direction was easier than forming a coherent research program, but does not explain that hiring was difficult because candidates had to resonate with an underdefined vision.
